counterfactual_missing_items: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable

Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses
He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers
decisive_items: PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen
Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable
Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears
response.rationale: C1 uniquely integrates the confirmed PVB19 infection with the cutaneous eruption: PVB19 DNA in lesional skin plus positive IgM/IgG directly link the virus to the skin lesions, while the ear/vermillion vesicles and papulocrusts provide the cutaneous phenotype. R1 captures the clinical pattern but omits the virologic proof; R3 confirms infection but lacks the cutaneous specification; R2 is contradicted by normal phototesting and no photosensitizer use; R4 does not fit the ear/vermillion vesicular distribution.

rejected.why: Phototoxic reaction is contradicted by unremarkable UV-A/UV-B phototesting and absence of photosensitizer exposure.
Gianotti-Crosti syndrome does not explain the ear/vermillion vesicles and lacks lesional PVB19 DNA support.
Subsumed by C1; serologic PVB19 evidence is less complete than C1's lesional DNA plus cutaneous phenotype.
